Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.

summaries.gardner: Capital One is a founder-led, well-known brand, but it is a mature lender in a slow-growing industry rather than a top dog in an emerging one. The stock is down about 6% over the past year and is not widely called overvalued, so it shows few Rule Breaker traits beyond its founder-CEO and the Discover network bet.
summaries.buffett: Card lending is understandable and Capital One has decades of underwriting know-how, a well-known brand and a founder who has run it since 1994. But returns swing with the credit cycle (net income fell from $12,390M in 2021 to $2,453M in 2025), it relies on leverage, and its moat is moderate, so it fits Buffett's approach only partly, mainly on price (about 1.1x book).
summaries.munger: Munger would value the simple economics of card lending and the rare issuer-plus-network position from Discover, but would worry about credit losses in a recession, regulatory risk such as a proposed 10% APR cap, and the leverage inherent in banking. It is a reasonable business at a fair price rather than a wonderful business.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would class Capital One as a cyclical stalwart with a clear post-merger story: Discover synergies of $2.5B targeted by 2H 2027 and moving cards onto its own network. With a forward P/E near 9 and analysts expecting about 17% EPS growth in 2027, its PEG looks attractive, though insiders are not buying.
summaries.fisher: Capital One has a long record of innovation in data-driven lending and technology (first big bank fully on the public cloud) and is unusually strong at marketing and acquiring customers. Margins have declined over five years and results depend on credit quality, so it only partly matches Fisher's growth-company points.
summaries.graham: A defensive Graham investor would like its size, ten years of profits, decades of dividends and a P/E times P/B near 15. It fails on earnings stability and growth: 2025 diluted EPS of $4.03 was well below 2023's $11.95, and the price is about 22 times average three-year EPS.
summaries.thiel: Capital One is not a monopoly built on proprietary technology ten times better than rivals; it competes in a crowded lending market. Owning the Discover network is a distinctive asset, but on Thiel's seven questions it scores mainly on team and distribution.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable compounders benefiting from big platform shifts, with efficient growth. Capital One's revenue jumped 37% in 2025 through the Discover acquisition, and Brex adds AI-driven spend management, but organic growth is modest and it is not a primary AI beneficiary.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller focuses on liquidity, rates and earnings momentum. Capital One's earnings should rebound as Discover costs fade and credit stays benign, but analyst estimates have recently drifted lower, the stock is down over the year, and its results are highly sensitive to the economy.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith wants high returns on capital without leverage, high gross margins and steady growth. As a leveraged lender with return on equity around 9% (TTM) and volatile earnings, Capital One does not fit Fundsmith's criteria, which exclude banks.
summaries.greenblatt: The Magic Formula excludes financial companies because their capital and earnings are not comparable, so Capital One is outside its scope. On simple measures its earnings yield is high (forward P/E about 9) but its return on capital is that of a bank.
summaries.akre: Akre's stool needs a great business, talented owner-operators and reinvestment opportunities. Capital One has a long-tenured founder and can redeploy capital into card growth and the Discover network, but the business is cyclical with moderate returns, so it fits partly.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai seeks simple businesses in temporary distress with low downside. Capital One is simple and trading near 1.1x book after a rough 2025, but the downside in a severe recession is meaningful for a leveraged subprime-heavy lender, so the heads-I-win case is only partial.
summaries.wood: Capital One is not a disruptive-innovation company in ARK's sense; it is a large incumbent lender. Its cloud-native technology and the Brex acquisition touch AI-driven finance, but it is not a leader in ARK's platforms.
summaries.ackman: Ackman looks for simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with high barriers to entry. Capital One is simple and has scale and a scarce network asset, but credit-driven earnings are not predictable and leverage is high, so it only partly fits.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep favoured 'scale economies shared' companies whose growing size lowers prices for customers. Capital One passes some savings on through no-fee banking and plans to cut network fees via Discover, but it is not a clear scale-economies-shared compounder.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed young companies attacking huge new markets with great technology. Capital One is a 30-year-old incumbent bank, so it falls outside his venture-capital approach.
summaries.nash: Nash's process favours fast-growing, cash-rich infrastructure plays with high margins. Capital One fails several of his instant kills (FY2025 operating margin about 4%, more liabilities than he allows) and scores about 70 on his 13 categories, though it looks cheap on forward P/E.

momentum.evidence: The share price was $201.74 on Oct 16, 2026, down 6.21% over 52 weeks and below about $220 a year earlier.

g4.evidence: Founder Richard Fairbank has led it since 1994 and institutions own about 88% of shares, but no famous investor is a notable backer.

g6.evidence: With a forward P/E of about 9.2 and a 24-analyst consensus of Buy with a $252 average target, the stock is not commonly called overvalued.

simple.evidence: It is mainly a card lender and retail bank (credit card segment 74% of Q2 2026 revenue), a business a careful generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: It has been profitable every year for a decade, but net income swung from $2,714M (2020) to $12,390M (2021) to $2,453M (2025).

integrity.evidence: The founder-CEO is long-serving and pay is tied to performance, but the 360 Savings rate case led to a $425M restitution settlement in 2026.

b6.evidence: The Discover ($35.3B) and Brex ($5.15B) deals were strategic (own network, corporate spend), but two large acquisitions in 12 months add integration risk.

roic.evidence: Return on equity was about 9% TTM and ROTCE 18.04% in Q2 2026, but returns rely on bank leverage (liabilities about 4.9x equity) and vary with credit costs.

fcf.evidence: As a bank, its operating cash flow ($31.45B TTM per StockAnalysis) mixes in lending flows, so free cash flow is not a meaningful measure of distributable profit.

b10.evidence: Tangible book value per share reached $105.21 at June 30, 2026, but EPS has not grown over five years ($5.18 in 2020 versus $4.03 in 2025) and the stock rose only about 34% in five years.

safety.evidence: At about 1.1x book value ($176.67 per share) and 9.2x forward earnings it is inexpensive, but credit-cycle risk limits the margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of 9.2 and PEG of 0.93 look reasonable for a lender expected to grow EPS about 17% in 2027.

mu5.evidence: Main failure paths are a deep recession, a federal APR cap (Trump called for a 10% cap in January 2026) or a botched network migration; it has survived 2008 and 2020.

reinvest.evidence: It can reinvest in card growth, Discover network expansion (Mexico, Caribbean, Canada, UK acceptance) and Brex, but at moderate bank-level returns.

ly2.evidence: It is a cyclical stalwart with a simple story: integrate Discover, capture $2.5B of synergies by 2H 2027 and move cards onto its own network.

ly3.evidence: Forward P/E of about 9.2 is below the roughly 17% FY2027 EPS growth analysts expect (PEG 0.93 per StockAnalysis).

runway.evidence: Growth avenues include network volume and corporate cards via Brex, but its core US card market grows at single digits (6.1% purchase-volume growth in 2025).

ly7.evidence: It is buying back stock (treasury stock rose $1,330M in Q2 2026 and diluted shares fell from 631.6M in Q4 2025 to 621.1M), but insiders hold only 0.76% and are not notable buyers.

ly8.evidence: It is widely covered by 24 analysts and held about 88% by institutions.

fi2.evidence: It keeps launching products (Venture X, Savor, no-fee 360 accounts) and added the Discover network and Brex spend platform.

fi3.evidence: Technology investment produced a cloud-native platform and data-driven underwriting, though benefits are hard to separate in results.

fi4.evidence: It is one of the largest US advertisers among banks and marketing rose 11% quarter on quarter in Q2 2026, supporting strong customer acquisition.

longterm.evidence: It accepted heavy integration costs and a 2025 profit hit to build a vertically integrated network, and spent years moving entirely to the cloud.

gr1.evidence: It had $673.8B of assets and a market cap of about $124B in October 2026.

ni10.evidence: It reported positive net income every year for the last decade, including $2,714M in 2020 and $2,453M in 2025.

gr4.evidence: It has paid a dividend every year since its 1994 IPO, including through 2009 and 2020 cuts, and paid $2.60 per share in 2025.

th1.evidence: Its underwriting and cloud stack are strong but not ten times better than JPMorgan, Amex or Citi.

timing.evidence: Buying Discover gives it a network as payments shift to digital, but card credit is late-cycle and rate-cap politics are a headwind.

team.evidence: Founder Richard Fairbank has led it for over 30 years, growing it into the largest US card lender by loans.
